prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant Z2 topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B018 as a single-part prize and I now also accept the narrower citation that most of you have converged on. The discovery is what the Secretary is supposed to look for first: a prediction that nature then confirmed. Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry gives a Z2-classified insulator with protected helical edge channels, a distinction by topology and not by broken symmetry. Molenkamp's group then measured edge conductance in HgTe/CdTe wells, and nearly two decades of transport, ARPES and STM work in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and bismuth-based materials has confirmed the picture. Nobody in the committee calls it premature. Round 1 sharpened rather than weakened the case, because it showed that the real work is in the wording. A citation that is explicitly about the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 class, with HgTe named, makes a claim that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp can carry, and it leaves the 3D materials as context. The same three names appear in every one of the six B018 configurations, so this is the least disputed attribution on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The credit gap is real and I do not want to talk it away. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal told Molenkamp's group which material to grow, Zhang died in 2018, and the three-dimensional case (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hsieh and Hasan) sits outside the trio. If the primary papers show that the HgTe experiment was essentially a realisation of BHZ, then Molenkamp's share would honour a verification of someone else's idea, and the citation would need to say so honestly. The 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions may also be read as having already covered the conceptual ground, and practical impact is still modest. I also repeat a limit on my own judgement: I am a string theorist and cannot judge the condensed-matter detail as well as Eriksson, Olsson and Mehlig can. If the committee, after expert review, concludes that the BHZ step was decisive and cannot be left out, B041 is the compact and cleanly attributed fallback, though I still have the novelty reservation about it.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B032 to B018, but asks whether Molenkamp's HgTe experiment is an independent discovery or only a realisation of the BHZ proposal, and whether the 2016 topological prize already covers the concept.
responses.response: Both objections deserve a straight answer. On BHZ, Kane and Mele had already predicted the quantum spin Hall effect in 2005 and the Z2 class that defines it, in graphene. BHZ in 2006 identified HgTe as a workable platform with a thickness-driven band inversion. Molenkamp's group then had to grow the wells, gate them and show conductance near 2e^2/h in short channels and its absence in wide ones. I think that is a genuine experimental discovery, because the prediction could have failed in practice, but I agree with you that the committee should have the experts read BHZ and the 2007 paper side by side before the vote. That is why I support HgTe in the citation: it states exactly what Molenkamp's share is for and no more. On 2016, Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz honoured topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type phases that need broken time-reversal symmetry or a magnetic field. A time-reversal-invariant insulator, protected by symmetry and spin-orbit coupling, is a different class. I would call it a successor and not a duplicate.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B018, sides with a narrow citation, and asks whether a revised multi-name IceCube credit exists and whether B018 is weaker than its vote count if the narrow citation cannot stand without BHZ.
responses.response: Thank you for the answer on 2016, which I think is the right one. On IceCube, my view is unchanged from round 1: the discovery of a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is first-rate, but I cannot construct a three-name credit that I could defend. Halzen alone is not enough, and a fair account would have to include people from the IceCube, AMANDA and DUMAND lineage who are not in the supplied names. I would only revisit B016 if the expert reports give a clear multi-person credit, and I note that NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane still rest on few events without independent confirmation by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD. As for your last question, I would not say B018 is weaker than the vote count, but I would say the count tells us less than the citation does. If a narrow citation is indefensible without BHZ, the committee should find that out from the primary papers before the ballot and not after.

responses.point: Kroll holds B041 first and says it is a change of regime for what clocks can observe, with a clean Katori-Ye credit, and that B018 would move to a close second if its allocation were convincingly resolved.
responses.response: I gave B041 my last place in the opening ballot and I have moved up considerably, in part because of your argument. I accept that a hundredfold gain in accuracy that resolves redshift across a millimetre is more than a refinement, and that a neutral-atom lattice at the magic wavelength is a different principle from a Paul-trap ion clock. I also agree that the null results on constants should not carry the citation. What still holds me back is that the concept is Katori's, the performance frontier is partly Ye's and the other groups, and the redefinition of the second is still pending. I do not think that is as clean as a theory prediction confirmed by an experiment. If the BHZ question is resolved in favour of the narrow citation I hope you will see B018 as the allocation that is resolved, and if not I would be glad to join you on B041.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers a narrow citation around the Z2 state and quantum spin Hall effect with HgTe, keeps the quantum anomalous Hall effect out, and treats B030 as a strong alternative for a later cycle.
responses.response: I agree with all three points and have adopted the narrower wording in this round. I would add one practical thing. Since you and Olsson know the condensed-matter literature best, I would ask you to say in the committee record, before the ballot, whether you consider the omission of BHZ and the 3D work a boundary or a flaw. I treat it as a boundary: the three-person rule forces one, and Kane and Mele's step is clearly the decisive one for the time-reversal-invariant class. On B030 I now lean your way and would not advance it. Twisted bilayer graphene is under a decade old, the pairing mechanism is open, and Bistritzer's separate share is hard to defend, so I withdraw my own three-name version in favour of waiting.

uncertainties: Whether the primary papers show BHZ to be decisive enough for the HgTe experiment that the committee should hesitate to credit Molenkamp, and I have only recalled this history from memory.

Whether the committee accepts a narrow citation naming the 2D quantum spin Hall state and Z2 class with HgTe, with the 3D work (Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan) and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang acknowledged as context and not credited.
How much novelty the committee grants B018 beyond the 2016 prize, and how much it grants B041 beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes, since my own judgement of these overlaps depends on the experts.
A two-part prize was raised by the chair and Lindroth, but I do not see a configuration that stays within three people and keeps both parts defensible, so I have not proposed one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B018, B041 or B016. My supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet work in string theory and gravity, not on any shortlisted candidate. I have no tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or Halzen. I would recuse myself if a candidate with a direct Uppsala connection came up, and I note that nothing in round 1 raised one. Unchanged from round 1.
